Pathology of the Lungs II
PATHO LE 3 · Trans 4B · Dr. Mesina · Must-Know / Should-Know Reviewer

Whole-Lesson Summary

This lecture covers:

  • Pulmonary infections – pneumonia and its morphologic and clinical-setting types, lung abscess, chronic pneumonia
  • Pulmonary disease in HIV
  • Diseases of vascular origin – pulmonary embolism, pulmonary hypertension, pulmonary hemorrhage syndromes
  • Lung neoplasms – epidemiology, risk factors, pathogenesis, types, precursor lesions, local and paraneoplastic effects, TNM staging, metastatic and mediastinal tumors
  • Diseases of the pleura – effusion and pleural tumors

  • Core contrast 1: Pneumonia = inflammation + consolidation. Pneumonitis = inflammation without consolidation.
  • Core contrast 2: Bronchopneumonia (patchy, bilateral, extremes of age) vs Lobar pneumonia (entire lobe, unilateral, 90–95% pneumococci) vs Interstitial / atypical (alveolar spaces free of exudate, viruses and Mycoplasma).
  • Core contrast 3: Small cell carcinoma (most aggressive, neuroendocrine, central, ectopic hormones, no precursor) vs Non-small cell (adenocarcinoma, squamous cell, large cell).
  • Core contrast 4: Solitary fibrous tumor (benign, no asbestos link, CD34+) vs Malignant mesothelioma (malignant, strong asbestos link, Calretinin+).

Must-Know Concepts Flagged in the Lecture

❗ Red-Exclamation Must Knows
  • Lung Cancer: No. 1 cause of mortality from cancer.
  • Oncogene = car accelerator. Tumor suppressor gene = car brakes. Mutations in p53, RB1, p16 → increased risk of lung cancer.
📣 Lecturer-Emphasized Points (sampling, all appear in their tabs)
  • Lungs are the most frequent site of infection of any organ.
  • Vast majority are URTIs caused by viruses.
  • Typical pneumonia organisms are easy to isolate from culture.
  • Atypical are difficult to grow.
  • Bronchopneumonia and lobar pneumonia both have bacterial causative agents.
  • Aspiration pneumonia has a fulminant and necrotizing course.
  • Smoking-related carcinomas arise by stepwise accumulation of oncogenic driver mutations.
  • About ⅓ of adenocarcinomas have gain-of-function mutations (EGFR, ALK, MET, RET).
  • KRAS in 30%.
  • Majority express TTF-1.
  • Large cell carcinoma = “wastebasket diagnosis”.
  • 50% connect to a large airway.

Introduction p.1

Why the lungs? Must Know

  • Respiratory tract infections are the most frequent diseases encountered in the lungs 📣
  • Lungs are the most frequent site of occurrence as far as infections of any organ is concerned 📣
  • Vast majority consist of upper respiratory tract infections caused by viruses 📣
    • Likewise, lower respiratory tract (lower airways down to alveoli) are commonly affected as well
    • E.g.
      • Pneumonia and respiratory tuberculosis are included in the top 10 causes of mortality in the Philippines (2021 and 2022)
  • Why are the lungs the most frequent site for infection? 📣
    • Respiratory tract is continuously exposed to contaminated air as we breathe
    • Nasopharyngeal secretions are aspirated during sleep
    • Underlying lung diseases render the lung parenchyma vulnerable to microbial pathogens
Key Differentiator: Pneumonia vs Pneumonitis
  • Pneumonia: inflammation + consolidation of lung tissue.
  • Pneumonitis: general term for inflammation of lung tissue (non-infectious or infectious) without the consolidation of the lung parenchyma.

Predisposing Factors to Pulmonary Infections p.1

Predisposing factorExamples / mechanism from the lecture
Loss or suppression of the cough reflexComa, anesthesia, neuromuscular disorders, drugs, or chest pain
Injury to the mucociliary apparatus
  • Either impairment of ciliary function or destruction of ciliated epithelium.
  • E.g. cigarette smoke, inhalation of hot or corrosive gases, viral diseases, chronic diseases or genetic disturbances
Decreased function of alveolar macrophagesAlcohol, tobacco smoke, anoxia or oxygen intoxication
Pulmonary congestion and edemaProvides a milieu for infections to set in
Retention and accumulation of secretionsE.g. cystic fibrosis and bronchial obstruction
Immunologic deficienciesTreatment with immunosuppressive agents, leukopenia
Chronic diseases—

A. Pneumonia p.2

Portal of Entry

  • Inhalation of infected air droplets
    • Carry a virulent microbe and traverses host defense barriers
  • Aspiration of infected secretions or objects from URT
  • Hematogenous spread from one organ to other organs can occur
    • Origin of infection is from a distant source, reaches the lungs through the bloodstream
Clinical CueBacterial colonization of the airways is the most common route.

General Pathophysiology of Pneumonia Fig. 2, p.2

Infectious agent, foreign substance, blood-borne organisms that enter the blood circulation or aspiration of gastric content
↓
Cause inflammation of pulmonary tissue affecting both ventilation and diffusion
↓
The alveoli fills with exudate
↓
Interferes with the diffusion of oxygen and carbon dioxide
Mucosal edema of alveolar membrane occur
↓
Causing occlusion of alveoli resulting in decrease alveolar oxygen tension
↓
Hypoxia occur with retention of carbon dioxide, shortness of breath, fatigue, crackles in lungs or decrease breath sounds

B. Types of Pneumonia Table 1, p.2

BasisTypes
Etiologic types
  • Infective: Viral, Bacterial, Fungal, Tuberculosis
  • Non-infective: Toxins, Chemical, Aspiration
Clinical
  • Primary / Secondary
  • Typical / Atypical 📣
  • → Organisms that cause typical pneumonia are generally very easy to isolate from culture
  • → Atypical pneumonia are those organisms which are difficult to grow on culture
  • Community Acquired → usual pathogens are Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus, Moraxella, Mycoplasma and viruses
  • Hospital Acquired → Gram negative bacilli: Enterobacteriaceae family (Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, E. coli)
Morphologic typesLobar Pneumonia · Bronchopneumonia · Interstitial Pneumonia
DurationAcute · Chronic

C. Morphologic (Anatomic) Classification of Pneumonia p.2–3

Must Know – Alveolar Pneumonias
  • Both bronchopneumonia and lobar pneumonia have causative agents that are bacterial in origin. 📣
  • Both under the microscope: suppurative inflammation / outpouring of neutrophils within the alveolar spaces.
  • Overlap of the two patterns may occur.

Bronchopneumonia vs Lobar Pneumonia Table 2, p.3

FeatureBronchopneumoniaLobar Pneumonia
Agents
  • Most common agents:
  • → Staphylococci after URTI, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenza in COPD
  • → Pseudomonas aeruginosa in cystic fibrosis
  • → coliform bacteria
  • 90–95% are caused by pneumococci (Streptococcus pneumoniae type 1, 3, 7, & 2)
  • Rare agents:
  • → K. pneumoniae (in elderly)
  • → H. influenzae, Pseudomonas and Proteus
  • → Legionella pneumophilia
Age / host 📣
  • Extremes of age
  • Secondary infection in individuals who are already sick
  • Middle age (20–50 y.o.)
  • Primary in a healthy adult
  • Males common
Organisms (synchronous) 📣Staphylococci, Streptococcus, Haemophilus influenza95% pneumococcus (Klebsiella)
Pattern 📣
  • Patchy consolidation
  • Around small bronchi
  • Diffuse randomly, usually starting at the basal portions of the lungs
  • Not limited by anatomic boundaries
  • Usually bilateral
  • Entire lobe consolidation
  • Diffuse
  • Limited by anatomic boundaries
  • Usually unilateral
  • Involves consolidation of either an entire segment or lobe of the lung
Origin
  • Represent an extension from pre-existing bronchitis or bronchiolitis
  • Extremely common, tends to occur in two extremes of life
  • Characteristic feature: Patchy consolidation of the lung
  • Acute bacterial infection of a large portion of the lobe or entire lobe is consolidated
  • Classic lobar pneumonia is now infrequent
Figure 4. Bronchopneumonia (left) and lobar pneumonia (right) [Synchronous Lecture] – p.3
Figure 3. Bronchopneumonia (left) vs lobar pneumonia (right): pattern of consolidation and actual gross appearance [Lecture PPT] – p.2
  • Notice: Bronchopneumonia = multiple scattered patchy foci, bilateral and basal.
  • Lobar = one whole lobe consolidated with a sharp anatomic boundary.

Interstitial Pneumonia p.3

  • Inflammatory reaction is confined within the interstitium and alveolar walls
  • Alveolar spaces are free of exudate
  • Viruses → E.g.
    • Influenza virus, RSV, Adenovirus, Mycoplasma pneumoniae

Lobar Pneumonia – 4 Stages of Inflammatory Response p.3

Widespread involvement of the entire lobe with widespread fibrinosuppurative consolidation.

Stage I: Congestion
  • The lung is heavy, boggy, and red.
    • The intra-alveolar space is filled with fluid.
    • The alveolar septal wall becomes permeable, hence few scattered neutrophils and numerous bacteria escape into alveolar spaces.
↓
Stage II: Red hepatization (solidification)
  • Alveolar spaces are filled with neutrophils, red cells (congestion) and fibrin.
    • Grossly the lung is firm/solid and liver-like.
↓
Stage III: Gray hepatization
  • Red cells are reduced due to lysis/disintegration but neutrophils and fibrin (fibrinopurulent/suppurative exudate) are still present within alveolar spaces.
    • Grossly, the lung is still firm/solid, non-crepitant with liver-like but the color has changed from reddish to gray to brown cut surface.
↓
Stage IV: Resolution
  • Exudates within the alveoli are being enzymatically digested, resorbed, ingested by macrophages or coughed up.
High-Yield Recap
  • Stage order: Congestion → Red → Gray → Resolution.
  • The “hepatization” stages share a firm, liver-like, non-crepitant lobe.
  • Red = RBCs still present.
  • Gray = RBCs lysed, neutrophils + fibrin remain.
Figure 5. Lungs, lobar pneumonia: gray hepatization (left), red hepatization (right) [Lecture PPT] – p.4
  • Notice: Lower lobes are expanded in both photos.
  • Red hepatization = diffused, dark, red consolidated, non-crepitant lobe (congestion and hemorrhage with fibrinosuppurative exudate).
  • Gray hepatization = congestion less prominent, RBCs lysed, leaving a fibrinosuppurative exudate that appears as a paler tan discoloration of the entire lobe.
Figure 6. Gray hepatization in Lobar Pneumonia [Lecture PPT] – p.4
  • Notice: Less RBC, more neutrophils and fibrin (pink threadlike material within the alveolar space).
  • Alveolar spaces filled with neutrophils and fibrinous exudate (green arrows).
  • Alveolar septae easily demarcated because of congestion of red blood cells.
  • Because of the exudates, alveolar spaces are airless, hence the lungs become solid (consolidation).

Bronchopneumonia – Morphology p.4

  • It begins as an acute bronchitis and spreads locally into the lungs
  • The lower lobes or right middle lobe are usually involved
    • Usually involves lower lobes (basal) because there is a tendency of secretions to gravitate into the lower lobes
  • Focal/patchy areas of consolidated acute suppurative inflammation in one or more lobes
  • Staphylococcus aureus is an important cause of secondary bacterial pneumonia after viral respiratory illness (e.g. measles in children and influenza in both children and adults)
  • Well developed lesions are 3 to 4 cm dry gray red ill-defined nodules
  • Microscopy: neutrophil-rich exudate filling the bronchi, bronchioles, and adjacent alveolar spaces
Figure 7. Bronchopneumonia: cut surface with multiple patchy whitish consolidated areas (left), microscopic picture with air spaces filled with inflammatory infiltrates (right) [Lecture PPT] – p.4
Notice the labels in the micrograph: distended alveolar spaces, vascular congestion, leukocyte exudation, acute bronchiolitis.

Clinical Features of Pneumonia p.4

  • Classical clinical presentation of bacterial pneumonia:
    • Sudden onset of high fever, chills, pleuritic chest pain and productive cough (mucopurulent sputum “rusty”), may be with hemoptysis
  • Reduced air entry and dullness by percussion in physical examination
  • When fibrinosuppurative pleuritis is present, it is accompanied by pleuritic pain and pleural friction rub
  • Blood test: leukocytosis with predominant neutrophils
  • Radiologic findings:
    • In lobar pneumonia: a radiopaque (consolidation) well circumscribed lobe
    • In bronchopneumonia: multiple small opacities, usually basal and bilateral

Complications

  • Tissue destruction and necrosis (abscess)
  • Spread of infection to the pleura leading to empyema
  • Organization of the exudate which converts the lung into solid tissue
  • Bacteremic dissemination to heart valves (infective endocarditis), pericardium, brain (meningitis), kidneys, spleen or joints (arthritis)
    • With the advent of better generation of antibiotics, complications are less seen.
      • However, a minor number of cases still succumb to complications of pneumonia

D. Clinical Setting Types of Pneumonia p.3

Community-Acquired Acute Pneumonia
Community-Acquired Atypical Pneumonia
Nosocomial Pneumonia
Aspiration Pneumonia
Chronic Pneumonia
Opportunistic pneumonias / Pneumonia in the immunocompromised host

Community-Acquired Pneumonia p.3

  • Definition: Lung infection occurring in individuals not recently hospitalized or in healthy individuals acquiring the infection from its normal environment
    • Any pneumonia acquired outside of a hospital, in a community setting
  • Usually follow a URTI
  • Can be lobar or bronchopneumonia (as to anatomic pattern of consolidation)
  • Etiology: mainly bacterial
  • May be subcategorized as atypical or typical in terms of ease of growth in the usual culture media

Causes

  • Most common cause of community-acquired acute pneumonia is Streptococcus pneumoniae
    • In some countries, like US, incidence is decreasing possibly owing to the administration of pneumococcal vaccines
  • Other common causes: H. influenzae · Moraxella catarrhalis · Staphylococcus aureus after URTI · Legionella pneumophila · K. pneumoniae · Pseudomonas aeruginosa spp
  • In intravenous drug abuser: S. aureus

More common in

  • Underlying chronic disease (e.g. DM, COPD, CHF)
    • COPD – H. influenzae and M. catarrhalis are the usual culprits 📣
  • Congenital or acquired immune deficiency
  • Decreased or absent splenic function
    • Spleen plays a role in filtering pathogens and produce immune responses against these bacteria
    • Loss of important immune cells such as macrophage, which are vital for recognizing and eliminating encapsulated pathogens
Clinical Cue – Organism by setting
  • After URTI → S. aureus.
  • COPD → H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis.
  • IV drug abuser → S. aureus.
  • Cystic fibrosis → Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
  • Elderly (lobar, rare) → K. pneumoniae.

E. Community-Acquired Atypical Pneumonia / Interstitial Pneumonitis p.4–5

Definition and Character Must Know

  • Characterized by patchy inflammation of the lungs confined to the alveolar septae and pulmonary interstitium and therefore is called interstitial pneumonitis
  • It is also called atypical because the inflammation is primarily in the alveolar spaces
  • Characterized by constitutional symptoms of upper and lower respiratory tract infections and can have a protracted clinical course with gradual resolution 📣
  • It lacks the typical finding of consolidation in chest X-ray and there is failure to isolate the pathogen using routine bacteriological methods 📣

Causative Organisms

Host / groupOrganisms
Immunocompromised hostPneumocystis carinii · CMV
Immunocompetent hostInfluenza A
The most common
  • Mycoplasma pneumoniae
  • → Sometimes referred to as walking pneumonia due to its milder symptoms compared to the typical pneumonia
  • → Affects young adults and occurs in clinical settings associated with closed living conditions like in schools and military barracks
Viruses
  • Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), Influenza virus type A and B, Human metapneumovirus, Adenovirus, Rhinovirus, Rubeola, Varicella, and SARS
  • → Produces similar morphologic changes wherein an interstitial inflammatory reaction is produced in the septal walls
Chlamydia spp.
  • (C. pneumonia etc.)
  • → Transmitted by inhalation of dried excreta of infected birds and causes ornithosis/psittacosis
Coxiella burnetiiQ fever

Morphology

  • Gross: Lungs are heavy but not firmly consolidated
  • Microscopic:
    • Septal mononuclear infiltrate
    • Alveolar air spaces either “empty” or filled with proteinaceous fluid with few or no inflammatory cells
Figure 8. Atypical Pneumonia [Lecture PPT] – p.5
  • Notice: Interstitial inflammatory reaction involving the walls of the alveoli.
  • Alveolar septae are widened or thickened, containing mononuclear infiltrates (lymphocytes, macrophages, occasional plasma cells).
  • Alveoli are free from exudates. When complicated by ARDS, thick hyaline membranes line the alveolar walls.
  • This pattern is usually due to pneumonia of viral etiology.
Key Differentiator: Typical (bacterial) vs Atypical (interstitial)
  • Typical: alveolar exudate (neutrophils) → consolidation on CXR.
  • Easy to culture.
  • Atypical: inflammation in septae/interstitium, alveoli free of exudate → no consolidation on CXR.
  • Difficult to culture.
  • Mononuclear infiltrate.

F. Coronavirus Infection p.5

  • RNA virus.
    • Weak pathogenic strains give rise to mild cold-like respiratory infection
  • Highly pathogenic strains are responsible to:
    • 2003: viral respiratory illness called SARS-associated coronavirus (SARS-CoV)
    • 2019: SARS-CoV2 whose pathogenicity is attributed to beta-coronavirus that binds to ACE2 protein found on the host target receptor on the surface of the pulmonary alveolar epithelial cells, explaining the tropism of the virus to the lungs

G. Nosocomial Infection p.5

  • Definition: Occurs 48 hours or more after hospital admission and is not present at the time of admission Must Know
  • Risk factors: Immunosuppression · Prolonged antibiotic therapy · Intravascular catheter · Patient with mechanical ventilator
  • Cause:
    • Gram positive cocci (e.g. Staphylococcus aureus)
    • Gram negative organisms like Klebsiella, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and E. coli

H. Aspiration Pneumonia p.5

  • Occur in markedly debilitated patients, comatose, alcoholic, or those who aspirated gastric contents either while unconscious or during repeated vomiting
  • These patients usually have abnormal swallowing or gag reflexes that predispose them to aspiration
  • Partly a chemical injury due to gastric acid and partly bacterial infection (anaerobic bacteria admixed with aerobic bacteria, e.g. Bacteroides, Fusobacterium, and Peptococcus)
Must Know 📣
  • This type of pneumonia has a fulminant and necrotizing clinical course.
  • Lung abscess is a common complication if the patient survives.

I. Lung Abscess p.5–6

  • Definition: Localized, suppurative, necrotic process within the pulmonary parenchyma Must Know
  • Features: tissue necrosis and marked acute inflammation
  • Organisms commonly isolated: Staphylococci · Streptococci · Gram negative organisms · Anaerobes
  • Pathogenesis:
    • Can follow aspiration of infective material
      • Seen among alcoholics, coma, anesthesia, or debilitated states with impaired cough reflex
    • As a complication of bronchopneumonia
    • Septic emboli
    • Tumors
    • Direct infection
Abscess originPattern
Due to aspirationUsually ends up in the right main stem bronchus and most often single
In the course of pneumoniaUsually multiple, basal, and diffusely scattered
Figure 9. Lung Abscess (Gross) [Lecture PPT] – p.5
  • Notice: Abscesses can be of varying size.
  • The cardinal histological change in all abscesses is suppurative destruction of the lung parenchyma within the central area of cavitation (Figure 10, p.6).

J. Chronic Pneumonia p.6

  • Definition: Disease caused by a microorganism and lasts up to 1 and half months, wherein the inflammatory reaction produced is mononuclear and most often a granulomatous inflammatory reaction
  • Due to slow growing microorganisms such as bacteria (e.g. M. tuberculosis) or fungi (Histoplasma capsulatum, Coccidioides immitis, Blastomyces)
  • In immunocompetent: Localized lesion with or without regional lymph node involvement
  • In immunocompromised: Systemic dissemination of causative agent accompanied by widespread disease
  • Chest x-ray: focal or diffuse shadows
  • Tuberculosis: most important entity within spectrum of chronic pneumonia

Pulmonary Invasive Aspergillosis p.6

  • Pulmonary lung infection associated with inhalation of conidia in post-transplant individuals
  • Incidence increased due to increasing number of immunocompromised patients in clinical practice with:
    • Solid organ & bone marrow transplantation
    • Increased use of corticosteroids & other immune modulating drugs
    • Infection with HIV virus
  • Histopathologic features:
    • Tissue invasion & cavitation due to tissue destruction
    • Presence of hyphae (narrow, dichotomous, branched at acute angles) in H&E stain
Figure 11. Pulmonary invasive aspergillosis on H&E stain, showing hyphae [Lecture PPT] – p.6
Notice: the narrow hyphae branching at acute angles.

II. Pulmonary Disease in HIV Individuals p.6

  • Spectrum of lung diseases associated with HIV
  • HIV infected: gradual but persistent loss of host immunity after infection → results in immune deregulation, dysfunction, deficiency
    • Alteration in several lines of defenses in lungs & respiratory tract, contributing to increased risk of lung complications:
      • Abnormality in mucociliary function
      • Abnormality in soluble defense molecules like defensins in respiratory secretions
      • Impairment of innate & adaptive responses within lung parenchyma → E.g. alveolar macrophages deficient in pathogen recognition
  • In HIV: chronic stimulation & activation of inflammatory cells in alveolar cells
  • Pulmonary diseases cause 30–40% of hospitalizations in HIV patients
  • Bacterial lower respiratory infections caused by usual pathogens are some of the most serious pulmonary disorders in HIV infection

Spectrum of Lung Infections and Complications in HIV Table 3, p.6

GroupOrganisms
BacteriaStreptococcus pneumoniae · Haemophilus spp. · Staphylococcus aureus · Pseudomonas aeruginosa
MycobacteriaMycobacterium tuberculosis · Mycobacterium avium complex
FungiPneumocystis jirovecii · Cryptococcus neoformans · Histoplasma capsulatum · Coccidiodes immitis · Aspergillus spp. (most often A. fumigatus) · Blastomyces dermatitidis · Penicillium marneffei
Must Know – CD4 Rule of Thumb
  • Bacterial & tubercular infections are seen with higher CD4 T-cell counts (>200 cells/mm³).
  • Pneumocystis jirovecii strikes when CD4 T-cells are ≤200 cells/mm³.

Pneumocystis jirovecii Pneumonia – Pathologic Key Feature Appendix, p.15

  • Pneumocystis jirovecii has “ground glass” opacities.
    • Stained with methenamine silver
  • Pathologic mark: Alveolar spaces filled with frothy and foamy exudate containing thick-walled cysts
  • Pulmonary infections are usually the most common type of tissue invasive infections involving an immunocompromised individual.
    • Pathogens may be usual common pathogens or opportunistic pathogens
Figure 31 (Appendix). Lung biopsy on H&E: (A) clear round structures are the cysts, (B) round/cup-shaped structures are the pneumocystis on Gomori methenamine silver – p.15
  • Notice: (A) characteristic frothy exudates harboring the organisms fill an alveolus.
  • (B) organisms appear round or cup-shaped, some show intracystic bodies.

III-A. Pulmonary Embolism p.7

  • Definition: Obstruction of pulmonary artery and/or one of its branches due to blood clot, fat, air, or tumor Must Know
  • Most common complications in hospitalized patients with prolonged immobilization – one of predisposing factors
  • Mostly embolic in origin
    • Arising from deep leg & deep pelvic veins (DVT), not superficial veins
REMEMBER: Virchow’s triad
  • Flow problems
  • Endothelial disruption
  • Hypercoagulability

Underlying conditions that predispose to embolism:

Cardiac disease
Long term immobilization
Cancer
Hypercoagulable states

Pathophysiology of Pulmonary Embolism p.7

Depends on: Extent of pulmonary artery blood flow obstruction · Size of occluded vessels · Number of emboli · Cardiovascular status of patient

Two pathophysiologic consequences

Respiratory compromise
  • Non-perfused lung tissue causing hypoxemia
Hemodynamic compromise
  • Due to increases in vascular resistance due to embolic obstruction
  • Obstruction in big vessel → atelectasis leading to decreased cardiac output
  • Obstruction in small vessel → less dramatic clinical outcome, but still decreased perfusion
  • Arterioles constrict due to platelet degranulation accompanied by release of chemical agents, resulting in bronchial & pulmonary vasoconstriction
    • This vasoconstriction plays a major role in hemodynamic instability that follows pulmonary embolism

Right-sided heart failure chain

Clot lodges, affected blood vessels in lung collapse
→
Increase pressure in pulmonary vasculature
→
Increase workload of right side of the heart
→
Heart failure (right sided)
Warning – Massive embolism
  • Massive embolism of the pulmonary artery can result in cardiopulmonary collapse from lack of perfusion, resulting in hypoxia & acidosis.
  • Results in hemodynamic instability and signals potential for imminent hemodynamic collapse and instantaneous death of the patient.

Morphology p.7

LesionFeatures in the lecture
Saddle embolusLodges at the main pulmonary artery bifurcation of pulmonary trunk
Pulmonary hemorrhage
  • Results from smaller emboli in the peripheral branches of the pulmonary circulation.
  • They can cause hemorrhage or infarction.
  • Intact bronchial circulation → adequate cardiovascular function → hemorrhage may occur but no infarction
Pulmonary infarct
  • Cardiovascular function is compromised.
  • Inadequate circulation.
  • Wedge-shaped and based on the pleura.
  • Early stages: hemorrhagic, raised red-blue area.
  • After 48 hrs: red cells begin to lyse and the infarct is paler and red brown in color
Key Differentiator: Hemorrhage vs Infarct
  • Intact bronchial circulation + adequate cardiovascular function → hemorrhage only, no infarction.
  • Compromised cardiovascular function + inadequate circulation → infarct (wedge-shaped, pleural-based).
Figure 13. Saddle embolus [Lecture PPT] – p.7
Notice: the embolus straddling the bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk (arrows).
Figure 15. Pulmonary Infarct [Lecture PPT] – p.7
Notice: the wedge-shaped, dark hemorrhagic area based on the pleura.
Figure 14. Pulmonary Hemorrhage [Lecture PPT] – p.7
Notice: peripheral hemorrhagic areas (arrows) from smaller emboli in peripheral branches.

III-B. Pulmonary Hypertension p.7–8

Must Know – Definition and values
  • Defined as a mean pulmonary artery pressure >25 mmHg at rest.
  • Normal: 12–16 mmHg at rest.

WHO Classification of Pulmonary Hypertension

GroupCategoryLecture notes
1Pulmonary arteriolar hypertension
  • Has something to do with enlarged pulmonary artery.
  • E.g.
  • Primary pulmonary hypertension specifically idiopathic hypertension typically occurring in women.
  • Includes some secondary hypertension that has something to do with collagen vascular disease, HIV, portal hypertension, and schistosomiasis
2Pulmonary hypertension due to left sided heart disease—
3Pulmonary hypertension secondary to chronic hypoxemiaRelated to lung disease which include COPD, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, sleep disease such as obstructive sleep apnea
4Pulmonary hypertension due to chronic thromboembolic disorders—
5Pulmonary hypertension with unclear and/or multifactorial mechanismsHematologic disorders, myeloproliferative disorders, sarcoidosis

Pathogenesis – Idiopathic Pulmonary Hypertension p.8

  • Have a genetic basis – autosomal dominant trait
  • Normally bone morphogenetic protein receptor type 2 (BMPR2) signals inhibition of smooth muscle proliferation and favors apoptosis
Germline mutation of BMPR2 gene
→
Absence of signaling
→
Smooth muscle proliferation
→
Thickening of pulmonary blood vessels

Morphology of Pulmonary Hypertension p.8

  • All forms of pulmonary hypertension whatever is the underlying cause are associated with medial hypertrophy of the pulmonary arteries and right ventricular hypertrophy
  • Plexiform lesion
    • Described as a web that spans the dilated thin walled arteries that can extend outside the vessel
    • Most prominent in familial or idiopathic hypertension
    • Pulmonary hypertension due to congenital heart diseases with left to right shunts
    • Pulmonary hypertension associated with HIV infection and drugs
  • Depends on the treatment or management of the underlying cause of patients with secondary pulmonary hypertension
  • Advance cases may lead to severe respiratory distress, cyanosis and right ventricular hypertrophy which leads to death from decompensated cor pulmonale
Figure 16. Normal Pulmonary Arteriole [Lecture PPT] – p.8
Figure 17. Thickened Arteriole, narrowed lumen [Lecture PPT] – p.8
Notice: compare the thin wall of the normal arteriole with the thickened wall and narrowed lumen in pulmonary hypertension (medial hypertrophy).
Figure 18. Plexiform lesion of small arteries [Lecture PPT] – p.8
Notice: the web-like lesion spanning the dilated thin-walled artery.

III-C. Pulmonary Hemorrhage Syndromes p.8

SyndromeLecture description
Idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosisListed in the lecture as a pulmonary hemorrhage syndrome
Goodpasture syndrome
  • Autoimmune disease in which kidney and lung injury are caused by circulating autoantibodies against the alpha-3 chain of collagen IV found on the basement membrane in the glomeruli and alveolar septae.
  • The pathogenic antibodies initiate inflammatory destruction of the basement in renal glomeruli and pulmonary alveoli, giving rise to rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and a necrotizing hemorrhagic interstitial pneumonitis.
Vasculitis-associated hemorrhage (e.g. hypersensitivity angiitis)Group of disorders which present with diffuse pulmonary hemorrhage and defined by the clinical triad of hemoptysis, iron deficiency anemia, and transient diffuse acinar infiltrates on chest x-ray
Figure 19. Goodpasture Syndrome in the Lungs [Lecture PPT] – p.8
  • Notice: focal necrosis of the alveolar walls associated with intra-alveolar hemorrhages.
  • At times the alveoli contain hemosiderin-laden macrophages.
  • In later stages (not shown): fibrosis thickening of the septae, hyperplasia of type 2 pneumocytes, and organization of blood in the alveolar spaces.

IV. Neoplasm p.9

  • Majority of cases of lung tumors are malignant
    • 90 to 95% of primary lung tumors are carcinomas
    • 5 to 10% are shared by carcinoid tumors and mesenchymal neoplasms
  • Primary: Benign (rare) · Malignant (very common)
  • Metastatic: neoplasm that has spread from its original site

A. Epidemiology p.9

❗ Must Know
  • Lung Cancer: No. 1 cause of mortality from cancer
  • Reason: Difficult to screen, many are asymptomatic, and clinical course is rapid such that majority of cases are diagnosed late and are in the advanced stage.
  • Leading cause of morbidity and mortality in the Philippines: 1.
    • Ischemic Heart Disease · 2.
    • Cancer (2017)
  • Most common cancers in the Philippines: Breast, lung, colorectal, liver, prostate
  • No. 1 cause of cancer in Filipino men
  • No. 3 cause of cancer in Filipino women after breast and cervical cancer
  • Sex ratio (M:F) is 1.5:1
  • In the US, lung cancer in males is decreasing while in females, the incidence is increasing
  • Age incidence: peak incidence is 55–65 years old
  • >90% of patients are >40 years old at the time of diagnosis

B. Risk Factors p.9

Tobacco / Cigarette Smoking (No. 1) Must Know

  • Remains as the top risk factor
  • Well-established carcinogen in the development of cancer with a direct linear correlation to the amount and duration of cigarette consumption
  • Increased risk (60x) among habitual heavy smokers (2 packs/day for 20 years) vs non-smokers
  • Women are more susceptible to carcinogens in tobacco smoke than men

Environmental Exposure

  • Industrial hazards: exposure to asbestos, arsenic, chromium, silica, nickel, and vinyl chloride
  • Air pollution: Adds risk to those who smoke or are exposed to secondhand smoke

Acquired Mutations

  • Smoking-related carcinomas of the lung arise by stepwise accumulation of oncogenic driver mutations that result in the neoplastic transformation of pulmonary epithelial cells 📣
  • Smoking acts as a driver effect that results in the mutation of the gene
  • Squamous cell carcinoma have the highest frequency of TP53 mutation while lung cancer in non-smokers (¾ are women) and usually adenocarcinoma is associated with EGFR mutation
Lecture-Specific Note (Appendix, p.16) – Etiological factorsSmoking is the number one leading cause · Industrial hazards · Air pollution · Chronic scarring

C. Pathogenesis p.9

Oncogenes
  • Gain of function mutation
  • Genes that cause cancer
  • KRAS, MYC family, Bcl-2, HER-2, and EGFR are involved in lung cancer
  • Mutation of oncogenes → activation/growth of cancer cells 📣
Tumor suppressor gene
  • Loss of function mutation
  • Genes that prevent cancer
  • p53, RB1, p16
  • Mutation/breakdown of tumor suppressor genes → no control of acceleration of oncogenes → proliferation of cancer cells 📣
❗ Must Know (lecture “Nice to Know” box)
  • Oncogene = car accelerator
  • Tumor suppressor gene = car brakes
  • → If you have tumor suppressor genes, you are less likely to have cancer.
  • → If you have problems such as mutations in p53, RB1, p16, then you have an increased risk of having lung cancer.

Molecular Pathogenesis of Lung Cancer Fig. 20, p.9

Tumor / groupMolecular features (from Figure 20)
Squamous cell carcinoma
  • Associated with smoking
  • Chromosomal deletion – 3p, 9p (site of CDKN2A gene) and 17p (site of TP53 gene)
  • Loss of expression of Rb tumor suppressor gene
  • Amplification of FGFR1
  • Inactivation of cyclin dependent kinase inhibitor gene – p16 protein lost
Small cell carcinoma
  • Strongly associated with smoking
  • Loss of function aberrations involving TP53 and Rb gene
  • Chromosome 3p deletions
  • Amplification of genes of Myc family
Adenocarcinoma
  • Gain of function mutations involving multiple genes encoding tyrosine kinase receptors – EGFR, ALK, ROS, MET and RET
  • Mutations in the KRAS gene in tumors without tyrosine kinase gene
Lung cancer in non-smokers
  • More common in females and are adenocarcinomas
  • Common mutations – EGFR
  • TP53 mutations – not uncommon
Inherited predisposition
  • Rare – found in Li-Fraumeni syndrome who inherit p53 mutations
  • First degree relatives – 2–3 folds increased risk
Figure 20. Molecular pathogenesis of Lung Cancer [Synchronous] – p.9
High-Yield Recap (Appendix, p.15)
  • Squamous: overexpression of TP53 and P53.
  • Adenocarcinoma: EGFR, ALK, ROS, MET, RET along with TTF-1.
  • KRAS in 30% of adenocarcinomas.
  • Small cell: inactivation of TP53 and RB.
  • RB loss-of-function is more closely associated with this diagnosis.
  • Non-small cell lung cancers associated with: EGFR, KRAS, BRAF, ALK, HER2, MET.

E. Precursor Lesions Giving Rise to Lung Cancer p.9

Precursor lesionDescriptionGives rise to
Squamous dysplasia and carcinoma-in-situ
  • Squamous metaplasia and dysplasia in the bronchial epithelium transforms into carcinoma in-situ.
  • This phase may last up to several years
Squamous cell carcinoma
Atypical adenomatous hyperplasiaCharacterized by dysplastic pneumocytes lining alveolar walls. Mildly fibroticAdenocarcinoma
Adenocarcinoma in situListed as a precursor lesionAdenocarcinoma
Diffuse idiopathic neuroendocrine cell hyperplasiaPrecursor lesions of neuroendocrine tumorsCarcinoid
Small cell carcinomaNo known precursor or pre-invasive phase

D. Types of Lung Cancer p.9

Must Know 📣These two broad classifications are based on the histology of the cancer cells which greatly affects approach and response to treatment.
Non-Small Cell Carcinoma – most common type (~85%, Fig. 32)
Adenocarcinoma (40%) → most common form. Most frequently found in women and non-smokers. Origin: alveolar type II epithelial cell
Squamous cell carcinoma (30%) → link to a history of smoking. Majority of cases start in the central portion of the lung. Origin: basal epithelial cell
Large cell carcinoma (15%) → rarest, 1 out of 10 cases. Grow quickly and are undetected until they metastasize. Origin: undifferentiated cells
Small Cell Carcinoma (~15%, Fig. 32) → less common but most aggressive among all the lung cancers. Origin: neuroendocrine cell
Figure 32 (Appendix). Classification of Lung cancer – p.16
Key Differentiator (Appendix, p.16): NSCLC vs SCLC behavior
  • Non-small cell: not that aggressive, slow-growing, early detection allows surgery as a good option.
  • Small cell: aggressive, silent behavior, detection already at the advanced/late stage.
  • Surgery is not a good option.
  • Treatment offered would probably be chemotherapy and radiotherapy.

Squamous Cell Carcinoma p.10

  • Occurs in males > females
  • Strongly associated with drinking (as written in the trans.
    • Elsewhere the lecture links squamous cell carcinoma to a history of smoking)
  • Harbors diverse genetic aberrations, many are chromosome deletions involving tumor suppressor loci
  • Arise along the airway of bronchi and presents as a hilar or perihilar mass on chest x-ray 📣
    • Exophytic growth: can grow as an intraluminal mass and cause obstruction
    • Endophytic growth: grows inward infiltrating the peribronchial tissues into the adjacent carina or mediastinum
  • Linked with mutations in TP53 and P53 protein overexpression, seen by immunohistochemical staining
    • P53 protein overexpression is a marker of TP53
  • Most often centrally located

Morphology

  • Gross: Cauliflower-like intraparenchymal mass
  • Histology: Keratinization or intracellular ridges
    • Squamous pearls or individual cells with markedly eosinophilic dense cytoplasm
Figure 21. Squamous cell carcinoma. Cauliflower-like intraparenchymal mass obstructs right main bronchus [Lecture PPT] – p.10

Adenocarcinoma p.10

Lecture-Specific Note
  • In the trans this block is headed “Large Cell Carcinoma”, but its content (glandular differentiation, TTF-1, EGFR/KRAS) and Figure 22 describe adenocarcinoma.
  • The true large cell carcinoma section follows on p.11.
  • Definition: Invasive malignant epithelial tumor with glandular differentiation or mucin production by the tumor cells
  • Peripheral in location
  • Typically seen in females and non-smokers.
    • Occurs in females > males
  • About ⅓ of adenocarcinomas have oncogenic gain-of-function mutations involving components of growth factor receptor signaling pathways such as EGFR, ALK, MET, and RET genes 📣
    • KRAS gene, present in 30% of adenocarcinomas
  • Majority of the tumor cells express Thyroid transcription factor-1 positive (TTF-1) 📣
    • TTF-1 is consistently expressed in the normal pulmonary airways
    • One of the most useful markers of epithelial lung tumors
    • Expressed in ¾ of adenocarcinomas
  • Precursor lesions include: Atypical adenomatous hyperplasia · Adenocarcinoma-in-situ
Figure 22. Adenocarcinoma. Ill-defined borders & near visceral pleura (L). Tumor cell attempts of glandular formation (R) [Lecture PPT] – p.10
Notice: peripheral location near the visceral pleura, and glandular formation by tumor cells.

Small Cell Carcinoma p.10–11

  • Most aggressive among all the lung carcinomas Must Know
  • Strongly associated with smoking.
    • Only 1% among non-smokers
  • Males = Females incidence
  • 70% of cases having metastasis at the time of diagnosis
  • No known pre-invasive phase
  • Most commonly associated with ectopic hormone production that gives rise to paraneoplastic syndrome
    • Excess ACTH due to carcinoma may manifest as Cushing’s Syndrome
  • Central or hilar tumor in location
  • Best treated with chemotherapy
  • Highest mutational burden among lung cancers

Morphology

  • Gross:
    • White, tan, soft, friable, and extensively necrotic tumor
    • When centered in a large bronchus, it may be involved in a circumferential fashion and/or spread widely beneath the normal mucosa
    • Bronchus may be totally occluded in the late stages
  • Histology (left image):
    • Relatively small cells with scant to almost indiscernible cytoplasm
    • Ill-defined borders, finely granular nuclear chromatin (salt and pepper pattern)
    • Cells, particularly the nuclei, are round, oval, or spindle-shaped, hyperchromatic, and demonstrates nuclear molding
  • Immunohistochemistry (right image): Chromogranin, Synaptophysin, CD56 markers suggest that this tumor originates from neuroendocrine progenitor cells
Figure 23. Gross morphology of small cell carcinoma [Lecture PPT] – p.10
Figure 24. Histological appearance of small cell carcinoma (L: H&E, R: neuroendocrine IHC) [Lecture PPT] – p.10

Large Cell Carcinoma p.11

  • Definition: Undifferentiated malignant epithelial tumor that lacks the cytologic features of other forms of lung cancer
  • A diagnosis of exclusion since it expresses none of the markers associated with adenocarcinoma (TTF-1, napsin A) and squamous cell carcinoma (p63, p40)
  • May either be centrally or peripherally located
    • 50% of cases may be found with a connection to a large airway 📣
  • Histology: cells have typically large nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and moderate cytoplasm
Must Know – “Wastebasket diagnosis” 📣If you cannot recognize it as squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma or small cell carcinoma, but you see the presence of large cells with architectural patterns, you can diagnose it as a large cell carcinoma.
Figure 25. Large Cell Carcinoma [Lecture PPT] – p.11

Carcinoid Tumor p.11, 17

  • Represent neuroendocrine tumors in the lungs
  • Not related to cigarette smoking (20–40% are nonsmokers)
  • Most patients are younger than 40 years old with equal sex incidence
  • Polypoid, intrabronchial masses, but may infiltrate bronchial wall and surrounding lung tissue
  • Slow-growing, low-grade malignant as opposed to the aggressive behavior of small cell carcinomas
  • May be centrally or peripherally located → Peripheral tumors = solid and nodular
  • Arises from neuroendocrine cells (aka Kulchitsky cells) seen underneath the bronchial epithelium
  • Lesions are capable of producing the classic carcinoid syndrome, characterized by intermittent attacks of diarrhea, flushing, and cyanosis

Bronchial Carcinoids (Appendix, p.17)

  • Somehow a non-small cell type of malignancy.
    • Low grade malignant tumor
  • Classified into two based on location:
    • Central bronchial carcinoids (more common) → may cause associated obstruction and infection.
      • Not that aggressive.
      • Low percentage of metastasis (usually 5%)
    • Peripherally rising carcinoids in the lungs
Figure 26. Carcinoid Tumor [Lecture PPT] – p.11
  • (L) Gross: carcinoids growing as spherical and pale polypoid masses that project into the lumen of the bronchus and are covered by an intact mucosa.
  • Some may penetrate the bronchial wall to fan out in the peribronchial tissue, producing a collar-button lesion.
  • (R) Histology: small, rounded, uniform nuclei and moderate cytoplasm.
  • Monotonous cells arranged as organoid, trabecular, palisading, ribbon or rosette-like tumor arrangement.

Immunohistochemical (IHC) Stains / Markers Appendix, p.16–17

  • Presently a very common request from pathologists in surgical pathology
  • Aids in the diagnosis especially when given very small biopsies that have a small portion containing undifferentiated/poorly differentiated tumor cells
MarkerFor
TTF1 and Napsin ASuspected adenocarcinoma
P40Non-small cell lung cancers: squamous cell carcinoma
CD56, Synaptophysin, ChromograninNeuroendocrine tumors: small cell carcinomas, bronchial carcinoids
MIB1 (similar to Ki67)
  • Cell proliferation: how aggressive, and the tumor behavior (prognostic wise).
  • High MIB1 = more aggressive tumor.
  • Does not tell the cell origin
Figure 34 (Appendix). Immunohistochemical (IHC) stains/markers: HE, TTF1, P40, CD56, Synaptophysin, Chromogranin A, MIB1 – p.17

Local Effects of Lung Cancer p.11

  • Cough is the most common manifestation of lung cancer
  • Unintentional weight loss of more than 10% over a short period may also occur
  • Patient may also complain of chest pain, hemoptysis, shortness of breath, or even symptoms relating to hypercalcemia, especially if dealing with squamous cell carcinoma

Paraneoplastic Syndromes p.11

  • Definition: Tumors that elaborate hormones or substances that produce non-metastatic systemic effects that accompany the malignant disease
  • Disorders caused by cancer but not directly a result of tumor invasion
Hormone elaboratedManifests asAssociated with
ADHHyponatremiaSmall Cell Carcinoma
ACTHCushing’s Syndrome
PTHRPHypercalcemiaSquamous Cell Carcinoma
CalcitoninHypocalcemiaAny lung cancer
GonadotropinsGynecomastiaSmall cell, Squamous cell & Adenocarcinoma

If you see X → think Y
  • Hyponatremia (ADH) or Cushing’s (ACTH) → Small cell carcinoma.
  • Hypercalcemia (PTHRP) → Squamous cell carcinoma.
  • Diarrhea, flushing, cyanosis → Carcinoid.
Exam Trap (Review Q4, p.14)
  • Adenocarcinoma elaborates gonadotropic secretion.
  • Inappropriate ADH secretion is seen in small cell carcinoma, not adenocarcinoma.

TNM Staging of Lung Cancer p.12

  • Direct relationship between clinical stage and survival rates particularly among non small cell carcinomas
  • Regarded by most as the single most important prognostic parameter in lung carcinoma
  • T: primary tumor size · N: regional lymph node involvement · M: presence of metastases
Primary Tumor Size (T)
Tis or T0Carcinoma in situ
T1
  • Tumor < 3 cm
  • No pleural or mainstem bronchus involvement
T2
  • Tumor >3 cm (3–5 cm)
  • Involvement of mainstem bronchus 2 cm from the carina, visceral pleural
  • Lobar atelectasis
T3
  • Tumor >5–7 cm
  • Involvement of the chest wall, diaphragm, mediastinal pleura, pericardium, mainstem bronchus 2 cm from the carina
  • Entire lung atelectasis
T4
  • Tumor >7 cm
  • Invasion of the mediastinum, heart, great vessels, trachea, esophagus, vertebral body, or carina
Regional Lymph Node Involvement (N)
N0No demonstrable metastases to regional lymph nodes
N1Ipsilateral, hilar, or peribronchial nodal involvement
N2Metastasis to ipsilateral mediastinal and subcarinal lymph nodes
N3Metastasis to: contralateral mediastinal or hilar lymph nodes · ipsilateral or contralateral scalene · scalene or supraclavicular lymph nodes
Presence of Metastases (M)
M0No distant metastasis
M1aSeparate tumor nodules. Malignant pleural effusion
M1bDistant metastasis
Figure 27. TNM Staging of Lung Cancer [Lecture PPT] – p.12
Notice the staging key in the figure: I – T1 N0 M0 · II – T1 N1 M0 · III – Tn N2 M0 · IV – Any M1.

Metastatic Tumors p.12

  • Since the lungs receive 100% of the systemic circulation through the right ventricle, secondary (metastatic) lung cancer is more common than primary lung cancer Must Know
  • Lung is the most common site for all metastatic tumors, regardless of the site of origin
    • Both carcinomas or sarcomas spread to the lungs either through the hematogenous (sarcoma) or lymphatic (carcinoma) route
    • Most metastatic lesions to the lungs are multiple, bilateral, and sharply outlined and are rapidly growing
  • Patterns of metastasis to the lungs:
    • Lymphangitic carcinomatosis → widespread neoplastic involvement of the pulmonary perivasculature and peribronchial lymphatics.
      • Seen in metastatic tumors from the stomach, breast, pancreas, and prostate
    • Penetration of intraparenchymal or nodal deposits into the wall of the major bronchus presenting as a polypoid intrabronchial mass → more often from breast, kidney, and large bowel
  • Most common cancers that metastasize into the lungs: breast cancer, followed by colorectal and renal cell carcinomas
  • The most common sites of metastasis of primary lung cancers are lymph nodes (hilar, regional), adrenal glands, liver, brain, and bones

Mediastinal Tumor p.12

  • Mediastinum: portion of the thoracic cavity located between the pleural cavities, extending anteroposteriorly from the sternum to the spine, and sagittally from the thoracic inlet to the diaphragm
  • Divided into superior, anterior, middle, and posterior compartments → proven useful since most cysts and neoplasms have a predilection for one compartment over the others
MediastinumTumors and other masses
SuperiorLymphoma · Thymoma · Thyroid lesions · Metastatic carcinoma · Parathyroid tumors
AnteriorThymoma · Teratoma · Lymphoma · Thyroid lesions · Parathyroid tumor
PosteriorNeurogenic tumors (Schwannoma, neurofibroma) · Lymphoma · Gastroenteric hernia
MiddleBronchogenic cyst · Pericardial cyst · Lymphoma

V. Diseases of the Pleura p.13

  • Most often a result of a secondary complication of an underlying pulmonary disorder
  • Primary disorders include: intrapleural infections · neoplasias → mesothelioma

A. Pleural Effusion p.13

  • Common manifestation of both primary and secondary pleural diseases, which may be inflammatory or non-inflammatory

B. Pleural Tumors p.13–14

  • Pleura may be involved by primary or secondary lesions
  • Secondary metastatic involvement is more common than primary tumors
  • Most frequent metastatic malignancy is arising from a tumor of the breast and the lungs
  • Two important primary tumors of the pleura: Solitary fibrous tumor (benign tumor) · Malignant mesothelioma

Primary Pleural Tumors Table 9 Must Know

ParameterSolitary Fibrous TumorMalignant Mesothelioma
NatureBenignMalignant
Association with asbestosNoneStrong
Gross
  • Dense fibrous tissue with occasional cyst filled with fluid
  • Well circumscribed but usually unencapsulated solid mass
  • Thick layer of soft, gelatinous gray-pink tissue encasing the lung
  • Thick, firm, wide pleural tumor that appears to ensheath the lung parenchyma
Histology
  • Whorls of reticulin and collagen fibers with spindle cells resembling fibroblasts
  • Proliferation of spindle cells with intermingling collagen bundles
  • No cellular atypia
  • Epithelioid – looks like adenocarcinoma
  • Sarcomatoid – looks like fibrosarcoma
  • Mixed (biphasic)
  • Mesothelial cells have a potential to develop epithelial-like cells or mesenchymal stromal cells
IHC stains
  • CD34 (+)
  • Keratin (−)
  • Keratin (+)
  • Calretinin (+)
Exam Trap (Review Q8, p.14)
  • Solid fibrous tumors are NOT associated with asbestos exposure. It is malignant mesothelioma that has a strong association with exposure to asbestos.
  • Asbestos exposure is the main cause of mesothelioma.

❗ Red-Exclamation Must Knows (lecture wording)
  • Lung Cancer: No. 1 cause of mortality from cancer → Reason: difficult to screen, many are asymptomatic, and clinical course is rapid such that majority of cases are diagnosed late and are in the advanced stage.
  • Oncogene = car accelerator.
  • Tumor suppressor gene = car brakes.
    • If you have tumor suppressor genes, you are less likely to have cancer.
  • If you have mutations in p53, RB1, p16, then you have an increased risk of having lung cancer.

Core Definitions

  • Pneumonia: inflammation + consolidation of lung tissue.
    • Pneumonitis: inflammation of lung tissue without consolidation
  • Bronchopneumonia: patchy consolidation, extension from pre-existing bronchitis/bronchiolitis, two extremes of life
  • Lobar pneumonia: acute bacterial infection where a large portion of the lobe or entire lobe is consolidated.
    • 90–95% pneumococci
  • Interstitial / atypical pneumonia: inflammation confined to interstitium and alveolar walls.
    • Alveolar spaces free of exudate
  • Nosocomial pneumonia: occurs 48 hours or more after hospital admission, not present at admission
  • Lung abscess: localized, suppurative, necrotic process within the pulmonary parenchyma
  • Chronic pneumonia: lasts up to 1½ months, mononuclear, most often granulomatous
  • Pulmonary embolism: obstruction of pulmonary artery and/or its branches by blood clot, fat, air, or tumor
  • Pulmonary hypertension: mean PA pressure >25 mmHg at rest (normal 12–16)
  • Paraneoplastic syndrome: tumors elaborate hormones/substances producing non-metastatic systemic effects.
    • Not a direct result of tumor invasion
  • Large cell carcinoma: undifferentiated malignant epithelial tumor lacking cytologic features of other lung cancers.
    • Diagnosis of exclusion.
    • “Wastebasket diagnosis”
  • Adenocarcinoma: invasive malignant epithelial tumor with glandular differentiation or mucin production

Mechanisms and Sequences

  • Pneumonia pathophysiology:
    • Infectious agent, foreign substance, blood-borne organisms, or aspiration of gastric content enters
    • → Inflammation of pulmonary tissue affecting both ventilation and diffusion
    • → Alveoli fill with exudate → interferes with O₂ / CO₂ diffusion
    • → Mucosal edema of alveolar membrane → occlusion of alveoli → decreased alveolar O₂ tension
    • → Hypoxia with CO₂ retention, shortness of breath, fatigue, crackles or decreased breath sounds
  • Lobar pneumonia stages:
    • Congestion → heavy, boggy, red.
      • Fluid, few neutrophils, numerous bacteria
    • Red hepatization → neutrophils + RBC + fibrin.
      • Firm, liver-like
    • Gray hepatization → RBC lysed, neutrophils + fibrin remain.
      • Non-crepitant, gray to brown
    • Resolution → exudate digested, resorbed, ingested by macrophages or coughed up
  • PE → right heart failure: clot lodges, vessels collapse → ↑ pulmonary vascular pressure → ↑ RV workload → heart failure.
    • Two consequences: respiratory compromise (hypoxemia) and hemodynamic compromise (↑ vascular resistance).
    • Arteriolar vasoconstriction from platelet degranulation drives hemodynamic instability
  • Idiopathic PHT: autosomal dominant.
    • Germline BMPR2 mutation → absence of signaling → smooth muscle proliferation → thickening of pulmonary vessels (BMPR2 normally inhibits SM proliferation and favors apoptosis)
  • Goodpasture:
    • Autoantibodies vs alpha-3 chain of collagen IV (glomerular and alveolar basement membrane)
    • → Destruction of basement membranes
    • → Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis + necrotizing hemorrhagic interstitial pneumonitis
  • Lung cancer pathogenesis: smoking → stepwise accumulation of oncogenic driver mutations.
    • Oncogene gain of function (KRAS, MYC, Bcl-2, HER-2, EGFR) → activation.
    • Tumor suppressor loss of function (p53, RB1, p16) → no control of oncogene acceleration → proliferation
  • Precursors: squamous metaplasia → dysplasia → CIS → SCC.
    • Atypical adenomatous hyperplasia → adenocarcinoma in situ → adenocarcinoma.
    • Diffuse idiopathic neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia → carcinoid.
    • Small cell: no known precursor

Important Values

Nosocomial: ≥48 h after admission Chronic pneumonia: up to 1½ months Bronchopneumonia nodules: 3–4 cm Lobar pneumococci: 90–95% Lobar age: 20–50 y CD4 >200: bacterial/TB CD4 ≤200: Pneumocystis HIV lung hospitalizations: 30–40% Infarct color change: after 48 h PHT: mean PAP >25 mmHg (normal 12–16) Lung carcinomas: 90–95% of primary tumors Carcinoid + mesenchymal: 5–10% M:F: 1.5:1 Peak age: 55–65 y, >90% are >40 y Heavy smoker risk: 60x (2 packs/day × 20 y) Non-smoker lung cancer: ¾ women, EGFR Adenocarcinoma: ⅓ GF-receptor mutations, KRAS 30%, TTF-1 in ¾ Small cell: 1% non-smokers, 70% metastatic at dx Carcinoid: 20–40% nonsmokers, central mets ~5% Weight loss: >10% Cough 50–75% · Hemoptysis 25–50% · Chest pain 20% T1 <3 cm · T2 3–5 cm · T3 5–7 cm · T4 >7 cm Li-Fraumeni relatives: 2–3 fold risk

Common Confusions and Exam Traps

  • Pneumonitis has NO consolidation. Pneumonia has consolidation (Review Q3)
  • Inappropriate ADH → small cell, not adenocarcinoma.
    • Adenocarcinoma → gonadotropins (Review Q4)
  • Patchy infiltrates + neutrophils + abscess → S. aureus bronchopneumonia (Review Q5)
  • Cushing’s + smoker + nuclear molding, scant cytoplasm → small cell carcinoma (Review Q6)
  • Solitary fibrous tumor is NOT asbestos-related. Mesothelioma is (Review Q8)
  • Plexiform lesion → pulmonary hypertension, not embolism/infarct/hemorrhage (Review Q2)
  • Lobar pneumonia initial pathway: bacterial colonization of upper airway descending to lower airway.
    • Aspiration of oropharyngeal secretions → lung abscess, right side (Formative Q1)
  • KRAS activating mutation → adenocarcinoma (Formative Q4).
    • RB1 and TP53 → small cell (Formative Q5)
  • Bronchial carcinoid behavior: slow-growing with potential for malignancy (Formative Q6)
  • Lymphatic route → carcinoma.
    • Hematogenous route → sarcoma
  • Bronchopneumonia = bilateral, not limited by anatomic boundaries.
    • Lobar = unilateral, limited by anatomic boundaries
  • Red hepatization still has RBCs.
    • Gray hepatization RBCs are lysed
  • PE arises from deep veins (DVT), not superficial veins
  • Hemorrhage (intact bronchial circulation) ≠ infarct (compromised circulation)
  • Large cell expresses none of TTF-1, napsin A, p63, p40.
    • MIB1 tells aggressiveness, not cell origin

Study Aids Study aid – derived from lecture lists

  • Lobar stages “C-R-G-R”: Congestion → Red hepatization → Gray hepatization → Resolution
  • Virchow’s triad “F-E-H”: Flow problems · Endothelial disruption · Hypercoagulability (lecture wording)
  • Small cell = “S” tumor: Smoking, Small cells with Scant cytoplasm, Salt-and-pepper chromatin, Synaptophysin, SIADH (ADH), Spread 70% at diagnosis
  • Squamous = “C” tumor: Central, Cauliflower, Cigarettes, hyperCalcemia (PTHRP), CIS precursor
  • Adenocarcinoma = “P” tumor: Peripheral, Patients who are women/non-smokers, Precursor AAH, TTF-1 Positive
